headline: Highest risk is medium: AutoGen can write and execute code in shared workspaces, while RisingWave’s interaction surface is undocumented, so pairwise conflicts and leakage are plausible but not directly evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and execute tool calls/code; if RisingWave outputs are placed in a shared workspace or piped into AutoGen, attacker-controlled content could be treated as instructions. RisingWave’s ingestion path is undocumented here, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents share a writable workspace or stdin/stdout bridge
IF RisingWave output is copied into AutoGen prompts or files without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic prompt ingestion from files
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages
Review any shared clipboard/stdin bridge before use

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and broad network egress, and it reads files from configured working directories. If RisingWave processes sensitive application data in a shared workspace, AutoGen could exfiltrate it through its outbound model/API calls. RisingWave’s own data handling is not documented, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF sensitive application data is stored in a directory AutoGen can read
IF AutoGen is configured to send that content to a third-party model provider
mitigations: Use separate directories with OS permissions
Redact secrets before handing files to AutoGen
Restrict AutoGen network egress to approved endpoints
Keep sensitive RisingWave data out of shared workspaces

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen has broad filesystem write and shell execution, while RisingWave is a data-engineering system that may also mutate shared data stores. Because neither profile documents locking or shared-resource coordination, overlapping writes are plausible; uncertainty again warrants medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, database, or pipeline state
IF no external lock or transaction boundary is enforced
mitigations: Assign disjoint write targets
Add file/database locking
Run one agent read-only during the other’s writes
Use transactional staging for shared artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen’s role-played agents and tool calls can generate outputs that another system may treat as authoritative. If RisingWave consumes those outputs as pipeline inputs or operational facts without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The interaction is not directly documented, so medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF RisingWave ingests AutoGen-produced text or records as trusted input
IF no validation step checks schema, freshness, or correctness
mitigations: Validate all inter-agent outputs against schema
Require human review for operational actions
Add checksum/version checks on exchanged artifacts
Log and diff inputs before downstream use

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen explicitly handles model-provider API keys and can send data to configured model providers, while RisingWave’s residency, retention, and certification posture is not documented here. No specific compliance mismatch is evidenced, but the pair could create policy gaps if sensitive application data is routed through AutoGen.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through AutoGen to a non-approved model provider
IF RisingWave data subject to stricter residency or retention rules is shared
mitigations: Classify data before sharing
Block regulated data from AutoGen prompts
Document retention and residency for exchanged artifacts
Use approved providers only
